title: Northrop Grumman Engineer Discusses Flight Support Booster Test
description: From Promontory, Utah, Northrop Grumman Ballistic Engineer Nik Ciastom, provides an overview of the Sept. 2, Flight Support Booster-1 (FSB-1) test. The flight support booster is structurally identical to each of the five-segment solid rocket boosters on the SLS rocket that produce more than 75 percent of the rocket’s thrust capability. The SLS solid rocket boosters are the largest, most powerful boosters ever built for flight. Each booster burns 6 tons of solid propellant every second and generates a max thrust of more than 3 million pounds. FSB-1 builds upon prior tests and will allow NASA and Northrop Grumman, the SLS booster lead contractor, to evaluate the motor’s performance using potential new materials and processes for future booster performance and flights beyond Artemis III.

This test, dubbed Flight Support Booster 1, or FSB-1,

Preparations for this test began in March.
The first of five segments was installed in the test bay in April

The motor has been cold conditioning

All of our large solid rocket motors
undergo ground tests at our Promontory site

In addition to holding this 1.6-million-pound motor in place,
the structure houses all necessary electronics and instruments
needed for motor firing
and gathering performance measurements.
Ground tests such as these
give us the opportunity to collect additional data parameters
on the performance of the motor
that would not be possible on a flight.
Upon ignition, the motor at this target temperature
will fire for about 122 seconds and produce 3.6 million pounds of thrust.
The five-segment SLS rocket booster
